summary: Count the straight, non-touching battleships ('X' cells in 1 x k or k x 1 lines) on a board.
mainInsight: Because ships are straight and never touch, each ship has exactly one top-left cell: an 'X' with no 'X' directly above and none directly to the left. Count those cells in one pass, with no extra memory and no mutation.
invariant: After scanning cell (i, j), count equals the number of ships whose top-left cell is at or before (i, j) in row-major order.

approaches.name: DFS / flood fill
approaches.summary: For each unvisited 'X', flood-fill its ship and add 1.
weaknesses: Extra memory or mutates the board

approaches.name: Count ship heads
approaches.summary: Count 'X' cells whose upper and left neighbours are not 'X'.
strengths: One pass, O(1) memory, board untouched
weaknesses: Relies on the straight, non-touching guarantee
approaches.interviewRelevance: The expected answer to the follow-up.

commonMistakes: Checking all four neighbours instead of only up and left (would miss ships).
Reaching for DFS and mutating the board when the follow-up forbids it.
Index errors on row 0 or column 0 without the i > 0 / j > 0 guards.
edgeCases: One ship spanning a whole row or column.

cards.answer: Count only the top-left cell (head) of each ship in one scan. Clue: Ships are straight 1 x k or k x 1 lines and no two ships are adjacent, so each ship has exactly one cell with no 'X' above it and no 'X' to its left.
keyPoints: Ships are straight 1 x k or k x 1 lines and no two ships are adjacent, so each ship has exactly one cell with no 'X' above it and no 'X' to its left.
cards.explanation: The guarantee turns component counting into a local test, which meets the one-pass, O(1)-memory, no-mutation follow-up.

promptVariants: Which guarantee would break the head-counting trick if it were removed?
The head-counting solution relies on one rule of the statement. Which one?
options: No two ships touch horizontally or vertically
The board has at most 200 rows and columns
Every board contains at least one ship
Ship lengths are bounded by the board size
cards.answer: No two ships touch horizontally or vertically
cards.explanation: If ships could touch, an 'X' with an 'X' to its left might be the head of a different ship, and the count would be too low. Straight shapes matter too: an L shape would have two heads.

incorrectOptionExplanations.The board has at most 200 rows and colum: Size affects running time, not correctness.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Every board contains at least one ship: That is not guaranteed (example 2 has none), and the trick works without it.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Ship lengths are bounded by the board si: Always true and irrelevant to the head test.

promptVariants: Why does the head test check only the cell above and the cell to the left?
Why not check the cells below and to the right too?
options: Row-major order reaches a ship's head cell first
Cells below and to the right are always empty
Checking four neighbours would cost O(m * n) extra
The right and lower cells are out of bounds at the head
cards.answer: Row-major order reaches a ship's head cell first
cards.explanation: A horizontal ship extends to the right and a vertical one downward, so only its first cell has no 'X' up or left. Checking right/down would reject heads of ships longer than one cell.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Cells below and to the right are always: They are 'X' for any ship longer than one cell.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Checking four neighbours would cost O(m: It is still O(1) per cell; the problem is wrong answers, not cost.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The right and lower cells are out of bou: Only at the border; heads usually have in-bounds neighbours.

promptVariants: Four single 'X' cells sit in the corners of a 3 x 3 board. Result?
cards.explanation: Each corner 'X' has no 'X' above or to its left, so all four are heads of single-cell ships.

incorrectOptionExplanations.1: They are not connected; each is its own ship.
incorrectOptionExplanations.2: That would pair the corners into ships, but '.' separates them.

promptVariants: Compare the DFS solution with head counting.
When would you still pick flood fill over head counting?
cards.answer: DFS counts connected components: O(m * n) time but O(m * n) memory for visited/recursion, or it mutates the board. Head counting is O(m * n) time, O(1) memory and read-only, but only works because ships are straight and never touch. For arbitrary shapes (Number of Islands) you need flood fill.
keyPoints: Head counting relies on the guarantee
cards.explanation: Knowing which guarantee unlocks the cheap solution is the transferable skill.

promptVariants: Time complexity of the canonical code on an m x n board?
Derive the running time of head counting.
options: O(m * n * k), k the ship length
cards.explanation: Each cell is visited once with at most two constant-time neighbour checks.

incorrectOptionExplanations.O(m + n): Every cell must be read; that is m * n cells.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(m * n * k), k the ship length: Ships are never walked; each cell does O(1) work.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O((m * n)^2): There is no pairwise comparison of cells.

promptVariants: Extra space of head counting: O(___).
Head counting uses O(___) extra memory and does not modify the board.
cards.explanation: Only a counter and loop indices are stored.
